A non-dealer's tsumo is not split equally three ways. The dealer pays double and the non-dealers pay half as much each. A non-dealer's tsumo at 30 fu 2 han is 1,000 from the dealer and 500 from each non-dealer, 2,000 in total.
Also, when a non-dealer deals in to the dealer, that one player pays 1.5 times what a non-dealer's win would cost.

mangan.definition: A limit hand worth 8,000 points for a non-dealer and 12,000 for the dealer. It applies at 5 han, or when the score calculated from fu and han would go above mangan.
mangan.usage:
Mangan is 8,000 points for a non-dealer and 12,000 for the dealer, and every 5 han hand is a mangan. Even at 4 han or less, if the basic points calculated from fu and han (fu times 2 to the power of (han + 2)) reach 2,000 or more, the score is capped at mangan. In practice that means 4 han at 40 fu or more and 3 han at 70 fu or more; only 30 fu 4 han (1,920 basic points) and 60 fu 3 han (also 1,920) fall short of mangan, at 7,700 points for a non-dealer.
Whether 30 fu 4 han and 60 fu 3 han are rounded up to mangan (kiriage mangan) depends on the rules.
mangan.caseStudy:
Riichi, menzen tsumo, pinfu and two dora make 5 han, a mangan: 8,000 points for a non-dealer (4,000 from the dealer and 2,000 from each non-dealer by tsumo) and 12,000 for the dealer (4,000 all).
Even a 4 han hand of yakuhai and three dora is 8,000 points if it has 40 fu, because its 2,560 basic points exceed the mangan line of 2,000. At 30 fu the same 4 han has 1,920 basic points and falls short of mangan: 7,700 for a non-dealer and 11,600 for the dealer.
mangan.pitfall:
4 han is not always a mangan. 30 fu 4 han is 7,700, short of mangan, and becomes 8,000 only at tables that play kiriage mangan. Conversely, even 3 han is a mangan at 70 fu or more.
Also, scores above mangan (haneman and up) are decided by han alone; fu does not matter.

haneman.definition: The scoring tier for 6 and 7 han: 12,000 points for a non-dealer and 18,000 for the dealer, 1.5 times a mangan.
haneman.usage: Haneman is the score of a 6 or 7 han hand: 12,000 points for a non-dealer and 18,000 for the dealer. It is 1.5 times a mangan, and fu does not matter. By tsumo, a non-dealer collects 6,000 from the dealer and 3,000 from each non-dealer, and the dealer collects 6,000 all.
haneman.caseStudy:
Riichi, menzen tsumo, pinfu, iipeikou and two dora make 6 han, a haneman. Honitsu (3 han closed), yakuhai and three dora make 7 han, also a haneman; both are 12,000 points for a non-dealer.
A 7 han hand at 2 honba is 12,000 + 600 = 12,600 points.
On a non-dealer's haneman tsumo, the dealer pays 6,000 and each non-dealer 3,000; on the dealer's haneman tsumo it is 6,000 all. Remember haneman as 1.5 times a mangan, and the pairs 8,000 to 12,000 and 12,000 to 18,000 come to mind at once.
haneman.pitfall:
Haneman covers both 6 and 7 han; 7 han is not a baiman. Baiman starts at 8 han.
Also, from haneman up you do not need to count fu. High fu or low, 6 han is 12,000 points.

baiman.definition: The scoring tier for 8 to 10 han: 16,000 points for a non-dealer and 24,000 for the dealer, twice a mangan.
baiman.usage: Baiman is the score of an 8 to 10 han hand: 16,000 points for a non-dealer and 24,000 for the dealer. It is twice a mangan, and fu does not matter. By tsumo, a non-dealer collects 8,000 from the dealer and 4,000 from each non-dealer, and the dealer collects 8,000 all.
baiman.caseStudy:
Chinitsu (6 han closed), riichi and menzen tsumo make 8 han, a baiman. An open hand with honitsu, toitoi, two yakuhai and three dora (9 han) is also a baiman.
Even 10 han is a baiman; sanbaiman starts at 11 han.
On a non-dealer's baiman tsumo, the dealer pays 8,000 and each non-dealer 4,000; on the dealer's baiman tsumo it is 8,000 all. Baiman is twice a mangan: 8,000 to 16,000 and 12,000 to 24,000.
baiman.pitfall:
8, 9 and 10 han are all the same baiman. 9 or 10 han does not raise the score.
Also, yakuman is not a yaku you reach by counting han. Apart from the counted yakuman that applies once you reach 13 han, yakuman yaku carry the yakuman score in their own right.

sanbaiman.definition: The scoring tier for 11 and 12 han: 24,000 points for a non-dealer and 36,000 for the dealer, three times a mangan.
sanbaiman.usage:
Sanbaiman is the score of an 11 or 12 han hand: 24,000 points for a non-dealer and 36,000 for the dealer. It is three times a mangan, and fu does not matter. By tsumo, a non-dealer collects 12,000 from the dealer and 6,000 from each non-dealer, and the dealer collects 12,000 all.
13 han or more is a counted yakuman (32,000 for a non-dealer), but some rules do not use counted yakuman and score 13 han or more as sanbaiman too.
sanbaiman.caseStudy:
Chinitsu, ittsu, riichi, menzen tsumo and two dora make 12 han, a sanbaiman. Chinitsu, riichi, ippatsu, menzen tsumo and three ura-dora also make 12 han, a sanbaiman worth 24,000 points for a non-dealer.
On a non-dealer's sanbaiman tsumo, the dealer pays 12,000 and each non-dealer 6,000; on the dealer's sanbaiman tsumo it is 12,000 all. Sanbaiman is three times a mangan: 8,000 to 24,000 and 12,000 to 36,000.
sanbaiman.pitfall:
Sanbaiman is 11 and 12 han; 10 han is a baiman. It does not start as soon as you pass 10 han in some vague sense; it starts exactly at 11 han.
Also, whether reaching 13 han makes a counted yakuman depends on the rules; at tables that do not use it, 13 han or more is still a sanbaiman (24,000 points).

kazoe-yakuman.definition: A hand without a yakuman yaku that scores the same as a yakuman because its han reach 13 or more: 32,000 points for a non-dealer and 48,000 for the dealer.
kazoe-yakuman.usage:
A counted yakuman gives a hand the yakuman score (32,000 for a non-dealer, 48,000 for the dealer) when its han add up to 13 or more, even without a yakuman yaku. Fu does not matter.
Whether it is used differs by rule set; where it is not, 13 han or more is a sanbaiman (24,000 for a non-dealer).
kazoe-yakuman.caseStudy:
Chinitsu (6 han), riichi (1 han), ippatsu (1 han), menzen tsumo (1 han), two dora and two ura-dora make 13 han, a counted yakuman. An open hand with chinitsu, toitoi, sanankou and four dora is also 13 han, a counted yakuman.
A counted yakuman is the same 32,000 points as a yakuman: 16,000 from the dealer and 8,000 from each non-dealer by tsumo.
kazoe-yakuman.pitfall:
A counted yakuman is not a yakuman yaku. Yakuman such as kokushi musou or daisangen do not combine with a counted yakuman (a yakuman hand does not count han at all).
Also, rules that make a counted yakuman a double yakuman are generally not used. Even 26 han is one counted yakuman, worth 32,000.

yakuman.definition: Yaku given a specially high fixed score, such as kokushi musou and daisangen. 32,000 points for a non-dealer and 48,000 for the dealer, with no build-up of fu or han.
yakuman.usage:
Yakuman is 32,000 points for a non-dealer and 48,000 for the dealer, and neither fu nor han are counted. Kokushi musou, daisangen, suuankou, tsuuiisou, ryuuiisou, chinroutou, shousuushii, daisuushii, suukantsu, chuuren poutou, tenhou, chiihou and others are yakuman.
Whether a table plays rules that make suuankou tanki, kokushi musou with a 13-sided wait, junsei chuuren poutou or daisuushii a double yakuman (64,000 points), or that add up several yakuman (combined yakuman), depends on the table.
yakuman.caseStudy:
Daisangen is a yakuman even when made by calling: 32,000 points for a non-dealer. Suuankou is valid only by tsumo; winning a pair wait by ron leaves three closed triplets, making a hand of sanankou and toitoi (with a single-tile wait, suuankou is valid even by ron).
A yakuman tsumo is 16,000 from the dealer and 8,000 from each non-dealer for a non-dealer, and 16,000 all for the dealer.
yakuman.pitfall:
A yakuman hand does not count dora or other yaku. Yakuman plus three dora does not raise the score (except when, under combined-yakuman rules, it overlaps with another yakuman).
Also, a yakuman is not 13 han. Counting han is what a counted yakuman does; a yakuman is a yaku with its own fixed score.

kiriage-mangan.definition: A rule that treats 30 fu 4 han (7,700 for a non-dealer) and 60 fu 3 han as mangan. Whether it is used depends on the table, and it is not standard.
kiriage-mangan.usage:
Kiriage mangan is a rule that treats 30 fu 4 han (7,700 for a non-dealer, 11,600 for the dealer) and 60 fu 3 han (7,700 for a non-dealer, 11,600 for the dealer) as mangan (8,000 for a non-dealer, 12,000 for the dealer). The same goes for tsumo: a 30 fu 4 han tsumo (2,000/3,900 for a non-dealer, 3,900 all for the dealer) becomes a mangan tsumo (2,000/4,000 for a non-dealer, 4,000 all for the dealer).
Whether it is used depends on the table's rules, and it is not standard.
kiriage-mangan.caseStudy:
A 4 han hand of riichi, menzen tsumo and two dora won at 30 fu is 2,000/3,900 for a non-dealer without kiriage mangan and 2,000/4,000 with it.
60 fu 3 han happens, for example, when a closed hand with three closed triplets of terminals or honors (24 fu from those triplets alone) wins by ron (20 + 10 + 24 = 54 fu, rounded up to 60 fu). With 3 han of sanankou and yakuhai, it is 7,700 for a non-dealer without kiriage mangan and 8,000 with it.
kiriage-mangan.pitfall:
Kiriage mangan is a separate rule from rounding up fu (bringing the fu to a multiple of 10). Rounding up fu happens under every rule set, but many tables do not use kiriage mangan.
It covers only 30 fu 4 han and 60 fu 3 han; 40 fu 3 han (5,200 for a non-dealer) and 50 fu 3 han (6,400 for a non-dealer) do not become mangan.

honba.definition: A counter that builds up when the dealer keeps the deal or a hand ends in a draw. Each honba adds 300 points to the winning score (100 points from each player on a tsumo).
honba.usage:
Each honba adds 300 points to the winning score. On a ron, the player who dealt in adds 300 times the number of honba; on a tsumo, each of the three players adds 100 times the number of honba.
The honba count goes up by one every time the dealer keeps the deal or a hand ends in a draw, and it goes back to 0 when a non-dealer wins (a dealer's win keeps the deal, so the count keeps building).
honba.caseStudy:
At 2 honba, a non-dealer who wins 30 fu 2 han (2,000 points) by ron receives 2,000 + 600 = 2,600 points from the player who dealt in. At 2 honba, a non-dealer who wins 30 fu 2 han by tsumo receives 1,000 + 200 from the dealer and 500 + 200 from each non-dealer, 2,600 in total.
A mangan's 8,000 points become 8,900 at 3 honba.
honba.pitfall:
Honba points are added on top of the score from the scoring table afterwards; they have nothing to do with han or fu. They are added even to mangan and above.
Also, the 300 honba points are paid by the player who dealt in (or by all three on a tsumo), and they are separate from the riichi sticks on the table (1,000 points each). The winner takes the riichi sticks that were placed on the table.

bazoro.definition: The mechanism that always adds 2 han to the han count when calculating a score. Also called banban. It is why the basic points are fu times 2 to the power of (han + 2).
bazoro.usage:
Bazoro is the + 2 in the formula for basic points, fu times 2 to the power of (han + 2). The calculation always adds 2 han to the actual han, so even a 1 han hand starts at 2 to the power of 3, a multiplier of 8.
The scoring table is the basic points from this formula, multiplied by 4 for a non-dealer's ron or by 6 for a dealer's ron and rounded up to the next 100.
bazoro.caseStudy:
The basic points of 30 fu 1 han are 30 x 2 to the power of (1 + 2) = 30 x 8 = 240; a non-dealer's ron is 240 x 4 = 960, rounded up to 1,000 points, and a dealer's ron is 240 x 6 = 1,440, rounded up to 1,500 points.
For 40 fu 2 han it is 40 x 2 to the power of 4 = 640: a non-dealer's ron is 2,560, rounded up to 2,600 points, and a dealer's ron is 3,840, rounded up to 3,900 points.
bazoro.pitfall:
The 2 han of bazoro are already built into the scoring table, so do not add 2 to your han yourself before looking up the table. For a 1 han hand, look at the 1 han column of the table.
Also, bazoro is neither a yaku nor dora, and it is not included when you announce your han.
